newsitem.title: USA: Christopher says successor must be forceful.
newsitem.headline: Christopher says successor must be forceful.

text.p: Secretary of State Warren Christopher, his resignation accepted by President Bill Clinton, said on Thursday his successor must be able to provide forceful, steady and determined leadership on U.S. foreign policy.
In an interview, he declined to name publicly his preference for the person who will soon take his place as America's top diplomat.

But asked about the qualities needed in a successor, he said: "It would be somebody who has the capacity to provide forceful leadership ... who has great tenacity ... who has a lot of endurance and stamina."

The job is challenging and hence "demands somebody who can project a policy of determination and activity without failing to be steady and calm," said Christopher, speaking in his cosy private office at the State Department moments before he was hailed by Clinton at a White House ceremony.

Former Sen. George Mitchell is believed by some administration officials to have the edge on replacing Christopher, but U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright is also said to remain in the running, as may be other candidates.
Clinton may make a choice known next week, officials said.
Christopher, who helped Clinton put together his first cabinet in 1992, discussed potential successors when he met with the president in Little Rock, Arkansas, on election night.

In the interview, Christopher, 71, said he would continue working hard -- on the Middle East, China, Bosnia and the State Department's critical need for more funding -- until he actually leaves office on Jan. 20, when Clinton is inaugurated for a second four-year term.
After that he will return to his home in California and to his old Los Angeles law firm, O'Melveny & Myers, as senior partner.

Mixing jokes with thoughtful answers, Christopher was interviewed in his shirtsleeves and displayed the more relaxed manner that has characterised his demeanor in recent weeks as announcement of his long-assumed resignation drew near.

On return to California, "first I'm going to see if I can stay in the same time zone for several weeks to see if I can get the body clock back" into sync, he said, laughing, in reference to travelling more than 700,000 miles (1,100,000 km) -- a record -- as secretary of state.

He said he would be active "on both the local and the international scene", but asked about possibly becoming a special presidential emissary on the Middle East, replied: "I think that's very unlikely and I don't envision that."

There is no issue on which Christopher has been more personally involved than Arab-Israeli peace efforts. He dearly wanted an Israel-Syrian deal, which is crucial to comprehensive regional peace and once seemed within grasp, but which is more elusive than ever.
Christopher did not dwell on the downside, saying: "It's been a wonderful four years. I'm very positive about where I am now" and feels what he hoped to accomplish has been done.
He described his approach to his job over four years as one of "steadiness and tenacity."

He said he takes satisfaction in seeing American values ascendant, bringing attention to global issues like non-proliferation and the environment, and helping make the United States "safer and more prosperous" with agreements like the comprehensive test ban treaty.
That is a big difference from his first two years in office, when he came under withering criticism for Clinton adminstration foreign policy failures, especially in Bosnia.

In fact in December 1994, Christopher discussed resigning and Clinton emissaries sounded out others -- retired Gen. Colin Powell, former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Democratic Sen. Sam Nunn of Georgia -- for the job.

Nevertheless, Christopher said: "Basically I'm not the resigning kind. I don't allow myself to get depressed. I'm not in the business of being depressed by ups and downs. You really have to see this as a long-term endeavour."
